[Penalized Regression: LASSO]{.custom-title}

[Grayson White]{.custom-subtitle} [Stat 243
Week 6 \| Fall 2026]{.custom-subtitle} ::: ::::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Announcements ::: {.nonincremental} - Group Project Preferences. Please fill out the [Google form](https://forms.gle/RNnH2AryRaiGLzdS9) by Thursday at 3pm. - More discussion of the group project scope on Friday. ::: ## Goals for this week :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.nonincremental .fragment} **Monday:** - Introduce **penalization** to improve MSE in regression models - Define and apply **Ridge Regression** in a case study ::: ::: ::: {.column width='50%'} ::: {.nonincremental .fragment} **Today:** - Introduce **LASSO** as a **penalization and variable selection** method - Apply LASSO in a case study ::: ::: :::: # The LASSO ## Recall: Least Squares and Ridge Regression Suppose we've selected a regression model: $$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_1 + \dots + \beta_pX_p + \epsilon,\qquad \epsilon \sim N(0,~\sigma^2)$$ :::: {.columns} ::: {.column .fragment .nonincremental} **Least Squares:** Find $\beta$s that minimize $$RSS=\sum_{i=1}^n\Big(Y_i - \hat{Y}_i\ \Big)^2$$ + Goal of RSS: Make regression line "close to data" ::: ::: {.column .fragment .nonincremental} **Ridge Regression:** Find $\beta$s that minimize $$ \textrm{RSS} + \underbrace{\lambda\sum_{j = 1}^p \beta_j^2}_\text{Ridge Penalty} \qquad \textrm{where } \lambda \geq 0 $$ + Goal of Ridge Penalty: Make coefficients smaller ::: :::: ## LASSO Regression $$\begin{aligned} \text{Least Squares: }& \text{Minimize RSS}\\ \text{Ridge Regression: }& \text{Minimize RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2 \end{aligned}$$ **Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator**: Find $\beta$s that minimize $$ \textrm{RSS} + \underbrace{\lambda\sum_{j = 1}^p \big|\beta_j\big|}_\text{LASSO Penalty} \qquad \textrm{where } \lambda \geq 0 $$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} + Goal of LASSO Penalty: Make coefficients smaller + Like Ridge, LASSO increases bias but decreases variance and (hopefully) MSE. So how is LASSO different from Ridge? ::: ## Consider: Different Distance, Different Emphasis $$\begin{aligned} \text{Least Squares: }& \text{Minimize RSS}\\ \text{Ridge Regression: }& \text{Minimize RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^2\\ \text{LASSO Regression: }& \text{Minimize RSS} + \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p \big|\beta_j\big| \end{aligned}$$ ::: {.nonincremental .small} 1. Suppose $\beta_j= -10$. Calculate $\beta_j^2$ and $\big|\beta_j\big|$, then explain why this shows that Ridge penalizes "big" coefficients more than LASSO. 2. Suppose $\beta_j= 0.1$. Calculate $\beta_j^2$ and $\big|\beta_j\big|$, then explain why this shows that LASSO penalizes "small" coefficients more than Ridge. 3. How much does each penalty **decrease** if $\beta_j$ moves from $10$ to $9.9$? What about from $0.1$ to $0$? 3. Hypothesize why LASSO might shrink coefficients to **exactly zero** more often than Ridge. ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html}
03:00
``` ::: ::: ## LASSO for Variable Selection We've just uncovered why LASSO is a variable "**selection operator**": ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Ridge *and* LASSO:** Coefficients are encouraged to shrink. ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Ridge:** Penalty gets relatively smaller as coefficients get smaller + No benefit of making small coefficients zero. ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **LASSO:** Penalty gets relatively larger as coefficients get smaller + Bigger benefit of making small coefficients *precisely 0*. + $\beta_j=0$ $\implies$ $X_j$ removed from model! + This is variable selection! ::: # Geometric Perspective ## Geometric Perspective: Two Types of Distance How to measure distance between a point $x=(x_1, \dots, x_p)$ and the origin $(0, \dots, 0)$? :::: {.columns} ::: {.column} ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Euclidean distance:** "straight line" distance: $$ \Vert x\Vert_2 = \sqrt{x_1^2 + \dots + x_p^2} = \sqrt{ \sum_{j=1}^p x_j^2} $$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - Most common: Result of the Pythagorean theorem - Also called the **$\ell_2$ norm** - **Ridge** uses $\big(\Vert x\Vert_2\big)^2$ to "shrink" coefficients ::: ::: ::: {.column} ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Manhattan distance:** "grid line" distance: $$ \Vert x\Vert_1 = |x_1| + \dots + |x_p| = \sum_{j=1}^p |x_j| $$ ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - the **$\ell_1$ norm** - **LASSO** uses $\Vert x\Vert_1$ directly for shrinkage ::: ::: :::: ## Geometric Perspective :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="65%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ::: :::: ## Geometric Perspective :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="65%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ::: {.nonincremental} - [$\Vert \beta \Vert_2 = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$]{style="color: red;"} ::: ::: :::: ## Geometric Perspective :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="65%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="35%"} ::: {.nonincremental} - [$\Vert \beta \Vert_2 = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$]{style="color: red;"} - [$\Vert \beta \Vert_1 = 3 + 4 = 7$]{style="color: blue;"} ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - **Takeaway:** Ridge and LASSO measure "distance" differently ::: ::: :::: ## Geometric Perspective II What does a circle of radius $r$ look like in the $\ell_2$ norm? ::: {.fragment} $$ \Vert \beta \Vert_2 = \sqrt{ \beta_1^2 + \beta_2^2 } \leq r $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ::: ## Geometric Perspective II What does a "circle" of radius $r$ look like in the $\ell_1$ norm? ::: {.fragment} $$ \Vert \beta \Vert_1 = |\beta_1| + |\beta_2| \leq r $$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-7-1.png){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ::: ## Ridge and LASSO in terms of $\ell_q$ norms In ridge regression, we seek parameters $\beta$ that minimize RSS plus the (squared) $\ell_2$ norm of $\beta$: $$ \textrm{RSS} + \lambda \sum_{i =1}^p \beta_i^2 = \mathrm{RSS} + \lambda\Vert\beta\Vert_2^2 $$ ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} Alternatively, we could seek parameters $\beta$ that minimize RSS plus the $\ell_1$ norm of $\beta$: $$ \textrm{RSS} + \lambda \sum_{i =1}^p |\beta_i| = \mathrm{RSS} + \lambda \Vert \beta \Vert_1 $$ We have now reconstructed ridge and LASSO regression in terms of $\ell_1$ and $\ell_2$ norms! ::: - In addition to shrinking coefficients, LASSO also happens to perform variable selection! ## Alternative Formulations Instead of thinking of Ridge Regression and LASSO as minimizing the sum of RSS and the shrinkage penalty, we can think of them as solving a restricted optimization problem: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} - For each $s \geq 0$, Ridge Regression seeks to minimize $\textrm{RSS}$ subject to $\Vert\beta\Vert_2^2 \leq s$ - For each $s \geq 0$, LASSO seeks to minimize $\textrm{RSS}$ subject to $\Vert\beta\Vert_1 \leq s$ ::: ::: {.fragment} Suppose $q$ is $1$ or $2$. For each $\lambda > 0$, there is exactly one $s \geq 0$ so that if $\beta$ minimizes $$ \textrm{RSS} + \lambda \Vert \beta \Vert_q^q \qquad $$ then $\beta$ minimizes $$ \mathrm{RSS} \qquad \textrm{ subject to } \Vert \beta \Vert_q^q \leq s $$ ::: ## Variable Selection with LASSO For LASSO, the solution to the optimization problem often lies on a vertex of the domain, which corresponds to a subspace where one or more parameters are $0$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-9-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-10-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Variable Selection with LASSO For LASSO, the solution to the optimization problem often lies on a vertex of the domain, which corresponds to a subspace where one or more parameters are $0$. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-12-1.png){fig-align='center' width=100%} ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Ridge vs. LASSO ::: {.nonincremental} **Similarities:** - Fast to estimate models (similar to Least Squares) - Shrink coefficients: Increasing bias but reducing variance and MSE ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} **Differences:** - **LASSO performs variable selection simultaneously**, Ridge does not. - LASSO generally outperforms Ridge when some coefficients are *truly* zero. - Ridge generally outperforms LASSO when *all* coefficients are truly *non-zero*. ::: # Case Study: Wine Acidity ## Wine Acidity We study a "classic" dataset on red Vinho Verde wines grown in Northern Portugal. ::: {.nonincremental} + $n=200$ different wines + $Y$=Fixed Acidity + $X$=9 physical properties of the wine (e.g., residual sugar, pH, etc.) and average quality rating ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} wine <- read_delim("https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/wine-quality/winequality-red.csv", delim = ";", escape_double = FALSE, trim_ws = TRUE) wine <- wine[1:200,-8] head(wine) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 6 × 11 `fixed acidity` `volatile acidity` `citric acid` `residual sugar` chlorides 1 7.4 0.7 0 1.9 0.076 2 7.8 0.88 0 2.6 0.098 3 7.8 0.76 0.04 2.3 0.092 4 11.2 0.28 0.56 1.9 0.075 5 7.4 0.7 0 1.9 0.076 6 7.4 0.66 0 1.8 0.075 # ℹ 6 more variables: `free sulfur dioxide` , # `total sulfur dioxide` , pH , sulphates , alcohol , # quality ``` ::: ::: ::: ## Wine Acidity: Response variable distribution ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} ggplot(wine, aes(x = `fixed acidity`)) + geom_histogram(color = "white", fill = "steelblue") + labs(title = "Distribution of Y (Fixed Acidity)", x = "Fixed Acidity") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-14-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Least Squares Estimates ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} model_ls <- lm(`fixed acidity` ~ ., data = wine) library(coefplot) coefplot(model_ls, intercept = F, sort = "magnitude") + theme_bw() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-15-1.png){fig-align='center' width=75%} ::: ::: **Q:** Which coefficients will LASSO shrink to 0? ## LASSO in `R` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="1-9|8"} library(glmnet) library(broom) grid <- 10^(seq(-4, 1, length = 1000)) x <- model.matrix(`fixed acidity` ~ ., data = wine)[, -1] y <- wine$`fixed acidity` lasso_mod <- glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1, lambda = grid) ``` ::: ## LASSO Estimates (ggplot2) Examine how LASSO coefficient estimates vary as $\lambda$ changes: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} tidied <- tidy(lasso_mod) %>% filter(term != "(Intercept)") ggplot(tidied, aes(x = lambda, y = estimate, group = term, color = term)) + geom_line() + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10^c(-4, -2, 0)), labels = c(".0001", ".01", "1")) + theme_bw(base_size = 10) + labs(title = "Coefficent estimates based on LASSO", x = expression(lambda ~ " (lambda)")) + guides(color = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-17-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## LASSO Estimates (base) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(lasso_mod, sign.lambda = 1, label = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-18-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Cross-Validation for Optimal Tuning Parameter To find the optimal tuning parameter, $\lambda$, we again use Cross-Validation ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column-fragment'} ```{.r .cell-code code-line-numbers="2-6|7-8|10-18"} set.seed(1010) my_cv <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1, lambda = grid, nfolds = 20) best_L <- my_cv$lambda.min reg_L <- my_cv$lambda.1se tidied <- tidy(my_cv) ggplot(tidied, aes(x = lambda, y = estimate)) + geom_line(color = "red") + scale_x_log10(breaks = c(10^c(-4, -2, 0)), labels = c(".0001", ".01", "1")) + theme_bw(base_size = 15) + labs(x = expression(lambda), y = "Test MSE") + geom_vline(xintercept = best_L, color = "goldenrod") + geom_vline(xintercept = reg_L, color = "steelblue") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-19-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.nonincremental .fragment} + Gray vertical line is optimal $\lambda$: Test MSE minimized at 0.4297. + (Ridge yields Test MSE of 0.4317) ::: ## Feature Selection What features did the best $\lambda$ **select?** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} s <- which(lasso_mod$lambda==best_L) names(coef(lasso_mod)[,s] != 0)[(coef(lasso_mod)[,s] != 0)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "(Intercept)" "`volatile acidity`" "`citric acid`" [4] "`residual sugar`" "chlorides" "`free sulfur dioxide`" [7] "`total sulfur dioxide`" "pH" "sulphates" [10] "quality" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.fragment .nonincremental} What features did the best $\lambda$ **not** select? ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} names(coef(lasso_mod)[,s] == 0)[(coef(lasso_mod)[,s] == 0)] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "alcohol" ``` ::: ::: **Why not Quality, Free Sulfur Dioxide, Residual Sugar, and Total Sulfur Dioxide?** ::: ## Back to the Least Squares Estimates ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} model_ls <- lm(`fixed acidity`~.,data=wine) library(coefplot) coefplot(model_ls, intercept = F, sort = "magnitude") + theme_bw() + labs(title = "Coefficient Plot") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: ## Back to the Least Squares Estimates ::: {.cell layout-align="center" output-location='column'} ```{.r .cell-code} model_ls <- lm(`fixed acidity`~.,data=wine) library(coefplot) coefplot(model_ls, intercept = F, sort = "magnitude") + theme_bw() + scale_x_continuous(limits = c(-.12, .18)) + labs(title = "Coefficient Plot (Zoomed In)") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](stat243_wk06wed_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){fig-align='center' width=960} ::: ::: LASSO removed only a *high variance* coefficient that was near 0. ## Recap ::: {.nonincremental} Today, we learned about... - LASSO as a penalization and variable selection method - Similarities and differences with Ridge **Next time** - Quiz - Discuss the project :::
